title: Future Value
subtitle: What will 1 million today become after 10 years?
openingQuestion: 100 million invested at an interest rate of 10%/year. After 10 years, how much will there be?
explanation: Future value answers: what will an amount of money today become if it earns a return steadily over many years? The formula is FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, and the power lies in the exponent, not the interest rate itself: interest gets added to the principal and then keeps earning on itself. 100 million at 10% over 10 years becomes 259 million, while simple interest would only give 200 million - the entire 59 million gap is interest earned on interest, and that portion grows larger over time.

diagram.label: Earning r each year, interest added to principal
Multiply by (1+r) raised to the number of years
The portion above simple interest is interest earned on interest

realWorldExample.description: A person who starts saving for retirement at age 25 with the same monthly amount as someone who starts at 35 will have a significantly larger account balance by age 60 - not because they contributed more money, but because the Future Value of compound interest had an extra 10 years to work.

quiz.question: What is the Rule of 72?
options: Subtract your current age from 72 to get the stock allocation you should hold
Multiply 72 by the interest rate to get total interest
Divide 72 by the interest rate to get the number of years for money to double
Divide 72 by the number of years invested to get the minimum required interest rate
quiz.explanation: Rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate the number of years for money to double. 8%/year → 72/8 = 9 years. 12%/year → 72/12 = 6 years. A quick mental shortcut.

quiz.question: Why does Future Value grow exponentially (not linearly) over time?
options: Because management fees decrease over time
Because market interest rates typically rise the longer you hold
Because compounding inflation inflates the nominal amount faster
Because each period's interest is calculated on both principal and prior interest
quiz.explanation: This is the essence of compounding: FV = PV × (1+r)^n - the exponent n causes the value to grow exponentially, unlike simple interest which only accumulates linearly. This is why time is the most important factor in long-term investing.

quiz.question: 100 million, compound interest of 10%/year, after 10 years - how much will it become?
options: ≈ 259 million (= 100 × 1.1 to the 10th power, compound interest)
200 million (= 100 + 100 × 10% × 10, simple interest)
110 million (only calculating one year)
1,000 million (= 100 × 10 years, multiplying straight by the years)
quiz.explanation: FV = 100 × 1.1^10 = 100 × 2.5937 ≈ 259 million. The figure 200 million is the result of simple interest - the 59 million gap is exactly the interest earned on interest, which simple interest misses.

quiz.question: At an interest rate of 9%/year, how long does it take for money to double, per the Rule of 72?
options: About 9 years (swapping the numbers)
About 8 years (= 72 ÷ 9, the Rule of 72)
About 6.5 years (= 72 ÷ 11, wrong interest rate)
About 11 years (= 100 ÷ 9, mistakenly using 100)
quiz.explanation: 72/9 = 8 years. This rule is just an approximation but accurate enough within the 6-12% interest range, and helps you estimate quickly without a calculator.

quiz.question: Two people each invest 50 million at 8%/year. Person A leaves it for 30 years, Person B for 15 years. How do the results compare?
options: A and B are equal since they have the same capital and interest rate
A ends up with exactly double B's amount since the time is double
A ends up with more than triple B's amount, even though time is only double
A beats B by about 50% since compound interest accumulates evenly
quiz.explanation: A: 50 × 1.08^30 ≈ 503 million. B: 50 × 1.08^15 ≈ 159 million. More than triple, not double - because n sits in the exponent, half the time never gives half the result.

keyTakeaways: Compound interest: interest on interest - the power of time
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 / interest rate

practicePrompt.question: You deposit 100 million dong at a compound interest rate of 8%/year for 3 years. What is the future value (FV) of this amount after 3 years?
options: FV = PV × (1+r)^n = 100 × (1.08)³ ≈ 125.97 million dong, thanks to interest compounding every single year
FV = PV + r × n = 100 + 8×3 = 124 million dong, calculating simple interest accumulated year by year
FV always equals PV = 100 million because a savings deposit doesn't change in principal value
FV = PV / (1+r)^n ≈ 79.4 million dong, since you need to discount the initial amount backward
practicePrompt.explanation: FV = PV × (1+r)^n = 100 × (1.08)^3 ≈ 125.97 million dong. This is the compounding formula: money today will be worth more in the future thanks to interest accumulating exponentially year over year, not linearly like simple interest.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Compound interest: interest on interest - the power of time

application.title: Calculate FV yourself
application.message: Take an amount of money you currently have, assume an expected investment return rate, and calculate FV after 10 and 20 years to see the power of compound interest over time for yourself.
application.secondary: Try comparing against simple interest to see the gap more clearly.

sections.text: If PV pulls future money back to the present, Future Value (FV) does the opposite: an amount of money today, invested at rate r for n years, will become how much? This is the tool for visualizing the true power of compound interest over time.

FV = PV × (1+r)^n. **Example:** 100 million dong invested at a compound interest rate of 10%/year for 10 years: FV = 100 × (1.1)^10 = 100 × 2.5937 ≈ 259 million dong. Under simple interest only (no compounding): 100 + 100×10%×10 = 200 million dong. The 59 million dong gap is exactly 'interest on interest' - the reward of compounding.

The Rule of 72 helps you estimate quickly: divide 72 by the interest rate %/year to get the number of years for money to double. At 8%/year: 72/8 = 9 years. At 12%/year: 72/12 = 6 years. This is a handy mental shortcut for sensing the growth speed of an investment without needing a calculator.

variables.name: Interest rate per period
variables.description: Must match n's unit of time

variables.name: Number of periods
variables.description: Sits in the exponent - this is why time beats interest rate

example.title: 50 million, 7%/year, left alone for 30 years
example.explanation: 7.6 times over, without contributing another dong. That same 50 million left for only 15 years yields 138 million - half the time never gives half the result, because n sits in the exponent, not as a multiplier.

sections.label: r is an average, not a promise
sections.text: The formula assumes each year exactly hits r. Real markets don't work that way: two portfolios averaging the same 7%/year but hitting gains and losses in a different order will produce two different final results, and very different ones if you're withdrawing money during a loss period. Use FV to visualize magnitude, not as a guaranteed number.

items: FV grows exponentially because in each period, interest is calculated on both the principal and interest already accumulated
A longer investment period has a much bigger impact than a slightly higher interest rate
FV is the main tool for retirement planning and long-term savings goals
A common mistake: using simple interest to estimate a long-term savings goal, underestimating its real value thanks to compounding

lines: FV shows most clearly one truth: starting early matters more than starting with a large amount.
The gap between simple and compound interest is exactly why compounding is often called the world's 8th wonder.
